sources_note: Source ids match meta.json where one exists; every case fact cites a URL in `citations` (ids S1..Sn).
method: Case-based reasoning. 20 documented drought-driven hydropower crises (1992-2024) were coded from cited sources: dates, warning time, actions with decision and effect dates, cost, outcome. Actions are grouped by how far ahead they must start. A country is matched to the 3 most similar past cases (one per country) on five fields Patronus already has or can label: hydro share, storage type, ENSO link, import interconnection, and warning lead.

buckets.label: Start 6+ months before the expected shortfall
buckets.why: Water saved, new capacity and new lines take months to years to count.

buckets.label: Start 3-6 months ahead
buckets.why: Emergency rentals, barges and fuel contracts usually take 1-6 months from decision to power, and often arrive late.

buckets.label: Start 1-3 months ahead
buckets.why: Uses capacity, lines and markets that already exist: imports, thermal dispatch, paid demand reduction, quotas, tariffs.

buckets.label: Under 1 month: crisis operations
buckets.why: Spreading a shortfall that can no longer be avoided: campaigns, scheduled cuts, protecting critical loads.

actions.title: Hold water early: cut reservoir releases or allocations, ring-fence an energy reserve, restrict exports when storage is low
actions.typical_lead_time: Decision takes days to weeks; the effect builds over months of lower releases, so it only helps if it starts well before the dry season ends.
actions.cost_range: No direct cash cost; the cost is the replacement generation for the water held back. Brazil 2021: relaxing hydraulic constraints and managing storage was credited with R$26.9 bn lower operating cost (ONS, BRA-2021). Chile 2021-22: reserve of 650 GWh later cut to 66 GWh (CHL-2021).
actions.evidence_summary: Chile 2021 decree built a reserve in Ralco, Laguna del Maule and Lago Laja; Brazil 2021 preserved about 4.1% of Southeast/Midwest stored energy; Norway 2022 export-limit backstop with no rationing. Kariba 2015 and 2024 show the failure mode: allocations were cut but overdrawn (ZESCO used 39% over its allocation in Mar-Jun 2015).
risks: Conflicts with irrigation and spill rules (Chile)
Export restrictions strain neighbours and markets (Norway debate)

actions.title: Structural fixes: firm capacity (thermal, solar+storage, wind), new interconnections, long-duration storage
actions.typical_lead_time: 14 months for an accelerated 519 km line (Vietnam 500 kV circuit 3) to several years (Colombia Guavio, 5-6 years late; Ghana 2.3 GW PPAs signed 2015, adequacy 2016-18).
actions.cost_range: Vietnam 500 kV circuit 3: about USD 916 m. Colombia 1992: more than USD 1,200 m mobilised to finish Guavio. NZ Lake Onslow pumped hydro: estimate rose to NZD 15.7 bn and was cancelled.
actions.evidence_summary: Fixes the next crisis, not this one. Vietnam raised north transfer capacity from 2.2 GW to about 5 GW; Uruguay's post-2008 wind build-out made the 2023 drought a cost problem, not a shortage.
risks: Take-or-pay overcapacity and debt (Ghana 2.3 GW signed in panic)
Fossil lock-in if the new firm capacity is coal or oil

actions.title: Fast solar and distributed solar procurement (utility-scale tenders, net metering, tax waivers on panels)
actions.typical_lead_time: Not measured in the cases. Zambia 2024 started in Jul-Aug 2024, after load-shedding had begun.
actions.evidence_summary: One case (Zambia 2024); effect on the crisis not measured. Solar does not cover night peaks without storage.
risks: Too slow for the current dry season

actions.title: Emergency rental capacity: containerised diesel/gas units, power barges, strategic reserves
actions.typical_lead_time: 3 weeks to first power when financing is in place (Kenya 2000, Aggreko) to 18 months (Ghana powership, signed Jun 2014, arrived Dec 2015). Ecuador 2024: barge awarded 1 Aug, running 17 Sep, but the land plants in the same tender were overdue.
actions.cost_range: Ecuador 2024: USD 114.3 m for a 100 MW barge over 18 months (about USD 87/MWh at full availability, derived estimate). Kenya 2000: USD 75 m financing. California Strategic Reliability Reserve: about USD 2.4-3.4 bn. Tanzania 2006: USD 140,000/day paid to Richmond for no power in time.
actions.evidence_summary: Often arrives after the rains: Brazil 2001 emergency plants mostly after the peak, Sri Lanka 2019 barges after cuts ended, Tanzania 2006 Richmond delivered nothing. Works when contracted early and competitively (Kenya 2000, California 2022: 554-1,416 MW in the Sep 2022 heat event).
risks: Opaque single-source procurement and scandal (Tanzania Richmond)

actions.title: Secure fuel and fix existing thermal plants (LNG/diesel/coal cargoes, pipeline gas, maintenance)
actions.typical_lead_time: About 1-3 months (Chile 2021 gas from Argentina sought Aug, from Oct; NZ coal imports +69% in 2021).
actions.cost_range: Uruguay 2023: about USD 1.5 m/day of fuel, USD 193.5/MWh combined-cycle cost. Sri Lanka 2019: fuel oil LKR 31.93/kWh vs hydro LKR 2.49/kWh.
actions.evidence_summary: The thermal fleet is the main backstop, but availability is the weak point: Ecuador 2009 had about 500 MW offline, Ecuador 2024 only 880 MW of about 2 GW fossil was running, Vietnam 2023 had about 4,200 MW of coal out.
risks: Fuel import bill and FX pressure
Utility losses (Sri Lanka CEB LKR 85.4 bn loss in 2019)
Emissions; restart of retired coal (Chile Ventanas 1)

actions.title: Emergency imports over existing interconnections
actions.typical_lead_time: Days to about 1 month when a line exists (Zambia 2024: about 410 MW by Jul 2024; Sichuan 2022: about 130 GWh/day within days).
actions.cost_range: USD 57.7/MWh (Uruguay from Brazil, 2023) to USD 183/MWh (Zambia 2015, vs 5 USc/kWh retail) to about USD 320/MWh (Brazil from Uruguay 2021, FX estimate).
actions.evidence_summary: Large when the neighbour is wet and the line is big (Uruguay 2023: over 50% of supply some mornings; Sichuan 2022). Small or unreliable otherwise: Vietnam 2023 2.7% of northern demand; Colombia cut exports to Ecuador in Apr and Aug 2024 when it was dry too.
risks: Neighbour is often in the same drought (ENSO hits regions together)
High price and utility debt (ZESCO interest cover fell to 1.4x)

actions.title: Dispatch all existing thermal early, out of merit order, to save water
actions.typical_lead_time: Immediate if units are available and fuelled; Brazil started in Oct 2020, 7 months before the crisis peak.
actions.cost_range: Brazil 2021: R$16.8 bn (about USD 3.1 bn, FX estimate) for thermal plus imports through Oct 2021. Colombia 2016: thermal generators lost about USD 250 m under a capped scarcity price.
actions.evidence_summary: Brazil 2021, Colombia 2016, Chile 2021, California 2021, Uruguay 2023 and NZ 2021 all avoided rationing with thermal carrying 28-74% of supply. Where thermal was degraded (Ecuador, Venezuela, Vietnam), it did not.
risks: Cost passed to tariffs or debt (Brazil flag-account deficit R$12 bn)
Generator losses if scarcity prices are capped

actions.title: Paid demand reduction: large-consumer reduction auctions, household savings bonuses, industrial self-generation
actions.typical_lead_time: About 1-4 weeks to launch (Brazil Aug to Sep 2021; California ELRP/DSGS 2022).
actions.cost_range: Brazil 2021 bonus: R$500/MWh saved (about USD 93/MWh, FX estimate) vs R$1,500-2,500/MWh for the thermal it displaced. California DSGS: USD 295 m over 5 years.
actions.evidence_summary: Brazil 2021: 5.6 TWh saved Sep-Dec 2021 (2.7% of consumption) plus 237 MW average industrial peak reduction. Colombia 2016: more than 140 MW of industrial self-generation.
risks: Low awareness (71% of Brazilians unaware of the bonus)
Pays for savings that would have happened anyway

actions.title: Mandatory consumption quotas with bonus/penalty (instead of blackouts)
actions.typical_lead_time: About 1.5 months from decision (Apr 2001) to effect (Jun 2001).
actions.cost_range: Brazil 2001: GDP growth -1 to -2 pp (central bank ex-ante); the World Bank judged quotas saved at least 1-1.5% of GDP vs blackouts.
actions.evidence_summary: Brazil 2001 only, but well measured: national consumption fell 16.7% (about 20% target) with no rolling blackouts.
risks: Needs meters and billing data (Venezuela 2010: only about 50% of Caracas metered)

actions.title: Scarcity tariffs and emergency surcharges
actions.typical_lead_time: About 1 month to approve (Zambia emergency tariff Oct to Nov 2024; Brazil scarcity flag Aug-Sep 2021).
actions.cost_range: Brazil 2021: R$142/MWh surcharge; consultants estimated R$180/MWh was needed. Zambia 2024: target about USD 15 m/month to fund imports.
actions.evidence_summary: Mostly cost recovery, not a measured demand cut: Brazil's flag account still ran a deficit; Zambia's emergency tariff under-collected (snippet-sourced). Colombia 2016 used scarcity prices to keep thermal running.

actions.title: Crisis chamber with legal powers (single decision body across ministries, regulator, operator)
actions.typical_lead_time: Days to weeks (Brazil GCE May 2001; CREG chamber 28 Jun 2021).
actions.evidence_summary: Enabled Brazil's 2001 quota scheme and 2021 scarcity flag; NZ reviews after 9 Aug 2021 blamed coordination for avoidable cuts.

actions.title: Published rotational load-shedding schedule (last resort, to protect the reservoir floor)
actions.cost_range: Ecuador 2024: USD 1,916 m, -1.4% of GDP (central bank). Vietnam 2023: about USD 1.4 bn, about 0.3% of GDP (World Bank). Colombia 1992: about 1% of GDP. Tanzania 2006: about USD 1.1 bn (US Embassy estimate).
actions.evidence_summary: Used in 14 of 21 cases. It balances the system and slows drawdown (Venezuela 2016: Guri's daily fall halved from 20 cm to 10 cm), but it is the most costly outcome. Ecuador 2024 reached 14 h/day; Zambia 2024 more than 20 h/day.
risks: Water pumping and health services fail if not protected
Unpublished or changing schedules multiply the cost

actions.title: Public savings campaign with clear targets (ideally tied to rewards and penalties)
actions.cost_range: Low (communication cost not reported in the cases).
actions.evidence_summary: Colombia 2016 'Apagar Paga': 1,179 GWh saved vs a 400 GWh goal, daily savings up to 5.88%. California 6 Sep 2022 text alert: demand fell more than 2,100 MW within 5 minutes. Campaigns without incentives (Venezuela, Vietnam, Sichuan) were not quantified.
risks: Fatigue if it runs for months

actions.title: Ordered curtailment of energy-intensive industry (mines, smelters, steel)
actions.cost_range: Lost industrial output (Venezuela SIDOR output -40% in 2010).
actions.evidence_summary: Venezuela 2010, Zambia 2015 (mine load -30%), Sichuan 2022 (industry cut-off 15-25 Aug to keep households supplied), Brazil 2001.

actions.title: Shorter public-sector work weeks, holidays, clock changes, voltage reduction
actions.evidence_summary: Used in Venezuela 2010 and 2016, Ecuador 2009 and 2024, Colombia 1992, Chile 2021. No case measured a saving; Colombia's 1992 clock change was judged marginal.

actions.title: Protect critical loads (hospitals, water pumping, key industry/export feeders)
actions.evidence_summary: Tanzania 2006, Vietnam 2023 (industrial parks prioritised, limiting FDI disruption), Zambia 2024. Not quantified.
risks: Equity: protected feeders shift cuts onto others

actions.title: Cloud seeding / artificial rain
actions.evidence_summary: Sichuan 2022 and Sri Lanka 2019: no measured effect on reservoirs.

cases.summary: El Nino drought, the worst in over 50 years of records, hit a system about 80% hydro. The thermal fleet was largely out of service, reservoirs had been mismanaged and the 1,000 MW Guavio project was years late. The result was about 11 months of daily rotating blackouts (up to 9 h/day in Bogota). The government declared an economic emergency, advanced clocks one hour and later restructured the sector (Laws 142/143 of 1994).

hydro_share_pct.note: Generation system about 80% hydro and 20% thermal (Ochoa, National Energy Commission). Valora Analitik gives hydro as about 72-73% of installed capacity.

cases.storage_note: Seasonal reservoirs (e.g. Penol-Guatape, Chivor), dependent on two rainy seasons a year. They were drawn down because operating rules were set by the utilities themselves, inside ISA.
cases.import_capacity_note: No operational interconnection. Completing the interconnection with Venezuela was part of the emergency plan.

warning.what: Intense drought from late 1991 with El Nino. CONPES nonetheless stated in 1991 and 1992 that there was no blackout risk, and in Feb 1992 the minister said rationing would last only a few weeks.
warning.basis: From the drought onset 'since late 1991' (Ochoa) to the start of rationing on 2 Mar 1992.

actions.description: Nationwide daily scheduled power cuts from 2 Mar 1992. They started in the afternoon and were extended to more hours, especially peaks.
actions.lead_time_basis: Announced in Feb 1992, started 2 Mar 1992.
actions.cost_note: Cambio: economy lost about US$630m (then-current dollars; search excerpt only, page returned 403). Fedesarrollo director: about 1% of GDP. Contraloria study: 'several points' of GDP.
actions.effect: Cut about 15% of daily national consumption. By mid-1992 cuts lasted up to 9 h/day in Bogota, 10 h on the Caribbean coast and 18 h in San Andres.

actions.description: 'Hora Gaviria': clocks advanced one hour from midnight on 2 May 1992 until 7 Feb 1993, to use more daylight. The idea came from then Foreign Trade Minister Juan Manuel Santos.
actions.lead_time_basis: Decision date not found.
actions.cost_note: Social disruption only (school and work routines, commuting in the dark).
actions.effect: No public study or evaluation shows any saving. Experts call the effect marginal, and many rural people ignored it.

actions.description: Economic Emergency declared and Decree 700 of 1992 issued. It mobilised more than US$1,200m (including an IDB loan) to finish the 1,000 MW Guavio project, gave temporary tax incentives for private generation and access to public grids, let the state take over utility debt, and authorised energy purchases from private parties.
actions.lead_time_basis: Exact dates not found.
actions.cost_note: More than US$1,200m was mobilised, mainly for Guavio. This is investment, not crisis loss.
actions.effect: Long-lead. Guavio was not online in time to end the 1992 rationing.

actions.description: Fast-tracked contracts to repair the out-of-service thermal fleet and to contract new thermal generation. Many plants declared available proved to be out of service when called.
actions.lead_time_basis: No dates found.
actions.cost_note: Not found.
actions.effect: Not quantified. Official reports first blamed thermal unavailability and reservoir management for about 80% of the crisis and drought for 20%; by late 1992 the shares were reversed.

actions.description: Power barges rented as emergency backup.
actions.lead_time_basis: No dates found.
actions.cost_note: Not found.
actions.effect: Journalist Juan Londono: the barges 'no sirvieron de nada' (were useless).

actions.description: Completion of the interconnection with Venezuela, which was under construction.
actions.lead_time_basis: No dates found.
actions.cost_note: Not found.
actions.effect: Not quantified.

outcome.blackout_or_shedding: Daily rotating cuts from 2 Mar 1992 to about Feb 1993: up to 9 h/day in Bogota, 10 h on the Caribbean coast, 18 h in San Andres. One columnist gives an April 1993 end.
outcome.gdp_impact: About 1% of GDP (Fedesarrollo director). About US$630m (Cambio). 'Several points' of GDP (Contraloria).
outcome.what_worked: The crisis forced structural reform: Laws 142/143 of 1994, creation of the CREG regulator and the UPME planning unit, private entry and a capacity charge (later the reliability charge). These are credited with avoiding rationing in 2016.
outcome.what_failed: Utilities set their own reservoir and maintenance rules. The thermal fleet was unmaintained and availability was reported falsely. Guavio was 5-6 years late. Official optimism (CONPES said no risk) and the clock change and barges gave little measurable benefit.

cases.summary: Failure of the Mar-May 2000 long rains, after several dry years, left 70%-hydro generation 25-30% below average and forced severe power rationing. An IDA/EIB-financed emergency power programme brought in rented diesel plants, including a 45 MW Aggreko plant delivered within three weeks.
cases.storage_note: Tana River cascade (Masinga reservoir upstream of run-of-river and small-storage plants).
cases.enso_note: 1999-2000 was a La Nina period. The sources read do not make this attribution, so treat it as unverified.
cases.import_capacity_note: Very limited. The sources read describe no import option, and the response relied on domestic rental thermal.

warning.what: Several years of recurring drought. A search snippet (not verified) says KPLC began rationing in Sep 1999.

actions.description: Nationwide power rationing by KPLC.
actions.cost_note: Rationing was estimated to cost about USD 10m/day in lost production and exports.
actions.effect: Generation was 25-30% below the historical average in Jun-Jul 2000. Firms cut staff.

actions.description: Emergency Power Supply Project financed by an IDA credit (USD 72m) and the EIB (USD 3m). Under the first contract (2000), Aggreko supplied a 45 MW, 11 kV diesel plant at Embakasi, Nairobi, for 10 months.
actions.lead_time_basis: First power reached the grid within three weeks of the contract's effective date (Aggreko).
actions.cost_note: USD 75m covers total project financing. A per-kWh price was not found. A separate emergency power subsidy (hydro vs fuel cost gap) was put at 0.8% of GDP in the 2000/01 budget.
actions.effect: The government expected generation to be close to peak demand by Nov 2000.

outcome.blackout_or_shedding: Severe rationing in mid-2000, with generation 25-30% below normal.
outcome.gdp_impact: 2000/01 real GDP growth was revised to 0.5% from a programmed 2.3% (drought overall, with power rationing a main channel). Rationing was estimated to cost about USD 10m/day. Drought spending was 3.2% of GDP above programme.
outcome.gdp_impact_basis: Revised projection minus programmed projection (0.5 - 2.3). This is a drought-wide effect, not power alone.
outcome.what_worked: Containerised diesel rental was very fast (3 weeks to first power) once IDA financing was in place.
outcome.what_failed: Heavy hydro dependence with no import option. Fuel-cost subsidies hit the budget (0.8% of GDP).

cases.summary: Exceptionally low inflows and capacity growth that lagged demand pushed Southeast/Midwest reservoirs to a 40-year seasonal low in March 2001. The government avoided rolling blackouts with a 9-month quota-based saving programme: a 20% reduction target, fines and bonuses, and threatened cut-offs. Households cut use sharply, and part of the cut persisted after the programme ended.

hydro_share_pct.note: Hydro was 94% of electricity generated and 81% of production capacity in 2000 (ONS 2011, cited by Costa & Gerard).

cases.storage_note: Large multi-year reservoirs in the Southeast/Midwest, refilled by austral-summer rains. The South had full reservoirs, but limited inter-subsystem transmission meant it could not supply much to the other subsystems.
cases.import_capacity_note: Some imports from Argentina were arranged in early April 2001 (source gives no volume). The main constraint was internal transmission between subsystems.

warning.what: Southeast/Midwest reservoirs at their lowest seasonal level in 40 years at the end of the wet season (March 2001). Levels were already low in 2000.
warning.basis: Months from the March 2001 reservoir low to the programme start on 4 June 2001 (Costa & Gerard).

actions.description: First package of measures in early April 2001: efficient light bulbs given out in low-income areas, a 15% consumption cut in federal public buildings, energy imports from Argentina, and new thermoelectric plants.
actions.lead_time_basis: Announced and started in early April 2001 (Veja, cited by Costa & Gerard).
actions.cost_note: No cost found.
actions.effect: Not quantified. It was insufficient: by late April it was clear that use had to fall to avoid blackouts.

actions.description: Electricity Crisis Management Chamber (GCE) created by provisional measure. It was the inter-ministerial crisis authority and issued 8 provisional measures, 15 presidential decrees and 92 resolutions in 2001.
actions.lead_time_basis: Created in May 2001, within the same month as the decision.
actions.cost_note: n/a
actions.effect: Governance vehicle for the quota programme and the industrial cutbacks (GCE Resolution no. 8).

actions.description: Mandatory individual quotas from 4 June 2001 in the Southeast/Midwest and Northeast (partly the North; not the South). A typical residential quota was 80% of the customer's May-Jul 2000 average; small consumers got 100% of baseline or 100 kWh. Fines applied per kWh above 200 kWh for customers over quota: 50% of tariff up to 500 kWh, 200% above. Repeat violators were threatened with 3-6 day cut-offs, which were rarely applied. Overall target: -20%. Quotas were raised in Dec 2001 and Jan 2002.
actions.lead_time_basis: Programme announced around 23 Apr 2001 (Globo, cited by Costa & Gerard). Started 4 June 2001.
actions.cost_note: Main cost was forgone consumption and output. World Bank: at least 1-1.5% of GDP saved compared with rolling blackouts. An IAEE paper puts the programme's rationing cost at 3.0% of GDP (different method).
actions.effect: National consumption fell 16.7% compared with the same period a year earlier (IAEE). Southeast average household use fell from 199 to 145 kWh/month (World Bank). In a utility sample, 98% of households cut use and the median cut was 34%. Residential use rebounded after Feb 2002 but stayed below pre-crisis trend.

actions.description: Sector-specific mandatory cutbacks for industry and commerce set by GCE Resolution no. 8, measured against Jun-Nov 2000 consumption. Firms could trade their allowances on the wholesale market.
actions.lead_time_basis: Resolution no. 8 was in force when the June 2001 Inflation Report was written. Programme start was June 2001.
actions.cost_note: Central Bank ex-ante estimate: -2.0 pp GDP growth with no inter-sector energy transfer, -1.0 pp with transfer, -0.8 pp under the Finance Ministry's optimal-transfer scenario.
actions.effect: Not measured in the sources read. Self-generation was 16.19% of consumption in 1999 and cushioned the impact.

actions.description: Bonus for consuming below quota, paid per kWh saved, up to 200% of tariff, and initially funded from fines. Fines raised too little, so in September 2001 a guaranteed bonus of 100% of tariff was added for quotas below 225 kWh.
actions.lead_time_basis: Part of the quota programme. The guaranteed bonus was added in Sep 2001.
actions.cost_note: No total bonus cost found.
actions.effect: The response was so large that fines could not fund the non-guaranteed bonuses.

actions.description: State company CBEE (Comercializadora Brasileira de Energia Emergencial) created on 29 Aug 2001 (MP 2.209 and Decree 3.900) to contract short-term emergency generation capacity, with authority until 30 Jun 2006. Costs were recovered from consumers through an 'emergency capacity charge' and an emergency-energy charge (ANEEL Res. 249/2002), popularly called 'seguro-apagao'.
actions.lead_time_basis: No commissioning dates found. ANEEL Res. 249 of May 2002 covered costs incurred through Dec 2002.
actions.cost_note: No total found. Initial CBEE capital was R$50m, later raised to R$850m. A 2002 press report says the emergency plants sold at R$280/MWh, up to 6x hydro cost (seen only in a search snippet). In 2004 CBEE fined emergency-plant developers about R$150m. An Instituto E+ study puts the combined cost of the 2001, 2013 and 2021 crises at US$55.1bn, mostly emergency thermal paid via charges; it gives no per-crisis split.
actions.effect: Mostly arrived after the crisis peak. Consumers paid for multi-year capacity contracts.

actions.description: Rolling blackouts, preferred by distribution utilities, were kept as a plan B. They were never needed.
actions.lead_time_basis: Not implemented.
actions.cost_note: n/a
actions.effect: Avoided.

outcome.blackout_or_shedding: No rolling blackouts. Mandatory quota rationing ran Jun 2001-Feb 2002.
outcome.gdp_impact: Central Bank ex-ante estimate: -1 to -2 pp GDP growth in 2001. World Bank: quotas saved at least 1-1.5% of GDP compared with rolling blackouts. IAEE: rationing cost 3.0% of GDP.
outcome.what_worked: Individual quotas with price incentives, heavy media repetition and a fixed known end date produced a fast cut of about 20% without blackouts. Allowance trading let energy shift to the industries that valued it most. Household efficiency gains persisted for years.
outcome.what_failed: Rules were complex and changed several times. Fines could not fund bonuses. Utilities lacked staff for cut-offs, and Rio de Janeiro banned them. Emergency thermal contracts came late and left consumers with long-lived charges. Underlying causes were investment lagging demand and weak transmission between subsystems.

cases.summary: Drought dropped the Mtera reservoir about 3 m below its 690 m minimum generating level, forcing 12 h/day rationing in Feb 2006 and again from Jun 2006. A rushed 100 MW emergency contract went to the unqualified Richmond Development Company. The resulting scandal brought down Prime Minister Lowassa in 2008.

hydro_share_pct.note: Mtera and Kidatu alone produce more than 50%. Hydro capacity of 381 MW against about 550 MW demand. More than two-thirds hydro was reported in 2011.

cases.storage_note: Mtera is the key regulating reservoir upstream of Kidatu, plus Kihansi. It was 687.35 m on 15 Feb 2006 and still 1 m below the 690 m minimum on 3 Jul 2006.
cases.import_capacity_note: No significant interconnection imports. The response relied on emergency thermal.

warning.what: Businesses were already running on backup generators: one hotel's power costs jumped from about USD 5,000 (Sep 2005) to USD 65,000/month (Oct 2005).
warning.basis: Months from the Oct 2005 backup-generation surge to formal rationing on 4 Feb 2006.

actions.description: Nationwide rationing: 60 MW from 4 Feb 2006, then 12 h/day on weekdays (7am-7pm, about 120 MW) from 15 Feb. After a two-month pause it resumed on 8 Jun 2006 at 80 MW, 12 h/day (6am-7pm).
actions.effect: About 120 MW shed on average (Feb 2006), and 80 MW from Jun 2006.

actions.description: Key industries, hospitals and airports were exempt from the June 2006 rationing.
5% tariff increase in Jan 2006. The World Bank said up to 28% was needed.

100 MW emergency contract with Richmond Development Company (40 MW promised by end-Sep 2006, 60 MW by Dec), signed about 30 Jun 2006. The company had no experience and no valid registration. The contract later passed to Dowans.
actions.lead_time_basis: Delivery was still pending in Jul 2006 and the promised dates were missed.
actions.cost_note: Payments of USD 140,000/day were remitted to Richmond. USD 300m of IMF debt-relief funds was available for emergency generation, so funding was not the constraint.
actions.effect: Failed to deliver in the crisis. A parliamentary probe led to the resignations of PM Lowassa and two ministers on 7 Feb 2008.

actions.description: Aggreko supplied 40 MW of rental power (2006-2008). In 2011's repeat drought it signed a USD 37m, 12-month contract for 100 MW (Ubungo and Tegeta), with fuel included.
actions.cost_note: The USD 37m is the 2011 contract (100 MW, 12 months, fuel included). No 2006 price was found.

actions.description: An additional gas turbine was planned at Ubungo.
actions.lead_time_basis: Officials said installation would take at least four months.

outcome.blackout_or_shedding: 12 h/day rationing in Feb-Mar 2006 and from 8 Jun 2006. Tanesco expected it to last to year-end.
outcome.duration_basis: Feb-Apr plus Jun-Dec 2006, per official forecasts. The actual end date was not confirmed.
outcome.gdp_impact: The US Embassy estimated a loss of USD 1.1bn, or about 9% of 2006 GDP, using a 2004 World Bank figure of USD 2/kWh for unserved energy (range 5-10%). This is a high-end estimate.
outcome.what_worked: Exempting critical loads. Aggreko rental capacity.
outcome.what_failed: Opaque single-source emergency procurement (Richmond) delivered nothing in time and left payment obligations. Tariffs stayed well below cost. IPTL (the earlier emergency IPP from the 1990s drought) was not researched here.

cases.summary: Ecuador's worst drought in 40 years (from Sept 2009) cut output at the Paute plant. Colombia restricted exports at the same time. Rolling cuts ran from 5 Nov 2009 to 20 Jan 2010 while the government bought or rented emergency thermal units and power barges and sought imports from Peru and Colombia.

hydro_share_pct.note: share of 19,109 GWh generated in 2008; Paute alone 1,075 MW, about 33% of 2008 energy

cases.storage_note: Paute (1,075 MW) is the core of the system; on 10 Nov 2009 its reservoir was at 1,968 m against a normal 1,991 m and a minimum of 1,965 m. The Mazar storage dam upstream (160 MW) was not yet online and was due Feb-Mar 2010.
cases.import_capacity_note: Interconnection with Colombia: about 500 GWh imported in 2008 (about 2.5% of supply, at times 5-10%). Colombia announced export restrictions at the end of Sept 2009. Imports from Peru were being negotiated in Nov 2009.

warning.what: Drought began in Sept 2009 and Colombia announced export restrictions at the end of Sept 2009. Cuts began 5 Nov 2009 with no public warning.
warning.basis: From late Sept 2009 (drought onset and Colombian restriction) to the first cuts on 5 Nov 2009

actions.description: Scheduled rolling blackouts nationwide. Wikipedia gives 2-6 h/day; a US cable gives up to 8 h/day (5-8 daylight hours, worst in Guayaquil/coast); AP in Dec 2009 gives up to 4 h/day. There were no cuts at Christmas or New Year.
actions.lead_time_basis: Started 5 Nov 2009 without prior announcement
actions.cost_note: See outcome for economic losses
actions.effect: The cuts covered a shortfall of about 7,000 MWh/day out of about 42,000 MWh/day of demand (about 17%) in mid-Nov 2009. By 22 Dec the deficit was about 10% of about 50,000 MWh on a working day.

actions.description: Decree 124 (6 Nov 2009) declared a 60-day state of exception for the electricity sector. It allowed public funds to be spent on fuel imports for thermal plants. The emergency was later extended.
actions.lead_time_basis: Decree issued one day after cuts started
actions.cost_note: No figure found in sources read
actions.effect: About 500 MW of existing thermal capacity was offline in mid-Nov 2009 and the rest ran below capacity

actions.description: Emergency purchases negotiated with Peru and Colombia. Colombia itself was restricting exports.
actions.lead_time_basis: No volumes or start date found
actions.cost_note: No figure found
actions.effect: Not quantified. Wikipedia says (citation needed) that imports from Colombia and Peru stopped in Feb 2010.

actions.description: Leased power barges, about 70 small generators bought from Cuba (for January delivery), and US turbines bought by a delegation that went to Houston on 11 Nov 2009. At least four fuel-fired units totalling 315 MW were being installed from 23 Dec 2009.
actions.lead_time_basis: From purchase/lease decisions around 11-13 Nov 2009 to the first 315 MW of units starting from 23 Dec 2009
actions.cost_note: The cables do not give barge or rental costs
actions.effect: 315 MW added from late Dec 2009. A Jan 2010 US cable credits rainfall, rationing and purchased/rented capacity together for letting Paute refill.

actions.description: Limits on night-time business hours and on evening sporting events
actions.lead_time_basis: Reported in a cable of 13 Nov 2009
actions.effect: Not quantified

actions.description: Post-crisis compensation: electricity bill discounts of 10% for residential and 20% for commercial users for three months from Feb 2010
actions.effect: Compensation only, not supply-side

outcome.blackout_or_shedding: Rolling cuts of 2-8 h/day from 5 Nov 2009 until indefinite suspension on 20 Jan 2010
outcome.gdp_impact: Government estimate $500M of losses; private analysts about $1bn (US cable, Jan 2010). The business federation estimated $1bn of commercial losses over 45 days. Quito Chamber of Commerce: up to $20M/day, with commercial output down 30-50%. No GDP % estimate was found.
outcome.what_worked: Rain, rationing and added rented/purchased thermal capacity together let Paute refill enough to end cuts within about 2.5 months
outcome.what_failed: No early warning to the public. Past dry-season tools (thermal plus Colombia/Peru imports) were not enough because about 500 MW of thermal was offline and Colombia restricted exports. Mazar storage was late.

cases.summary: Drought plus years of demand growth outpacing new generation drew down the Guri reservoir towards its 240 m collapse level. Venezuela curtailed heavy industry, imposed rolling cuts outside Caracas, declared an electricity emergency (Decree 7,228, Feb 2010) with household surcharges, and launched a crash thermal build. Rains and new thermal ended rationing on 10-11 Jun 2010.
cases.storage_note: Guri (about 10,000 MW) is a very large reservoir. Its level was 265.77 m on 1 Nov 2009 and 258.08 m on 1 Feb 2010, against a critical 240 m below which units fail and about 70% of capacity is lost.
cases.import_capacity_note: No material imports in 2010. Imports from Colombia (Isagen) began only in 2011. Brazil offered technical help, not power.

warning.what: Guri falling steadily from 265.77 m (1 Nov 2009). SIDOR steel was capped at 300 MW in Dec 2009. Wikipedia cites an emergency decree of 21 Dec 2009.
warning.basis: From Nov 2009 drawdown and the Dec 2009 industrial cap to Jan 2010 national rationing

actions.description: Steelmaker SIDOR capped at 300 MW (from 800 MW) in Dec 2009. Industry was ordered to cut use by 20% or face cutoffs.
actions.lead_time_basis: Immediate administrative cap
actions.cost_note: SIDOR imported 30,000 t of billets from Brazil to compensate
actions.effect: SIDOR output fell 40% and it ran at 45% of capacity by Feb 2010

actions.description: Rolling cuts outside Caracas from Jan 2010: about 3 h every 3-4 days before Holy Week, then about 4 h/day. A Caracas plan was repealed on 13 Jan 2010 after less than 24 h. Cuts were lifted on weekends, holidays and off-peak hours on 22 May 2010, and suspended on 10-11 Jun 2010.
actions.lead_time_basis: Immediate
actions.effect: Actual demand reduction Jan-Feb 2010 was about 3%, against a 20% target

actions.description: Decree 7,228 (8 Feb 2010) declared a 60-day electricity emergency with extraordinary powers for the minister. Households above 500 kWh/month had to cut 10% from the same month of 2009, effective 9 Feb 2010, or pay a 75% surcharge, rising to fines of 100-200% for increases. Cuts of 10-20% earned a 25% discount and cuts above 20% a 50% discount. Commercial users above 25 kW faced a warning, then a 23-48 h cutoff, then permanent suspension.
actions.lead_time_basis: Effective the day after the decree
actions.cost_note: Caracas tariffs had been unchanged since 2002. Only about 50% of Caracas consumers had meters, which limited enforcement.
actions.effect: Not separately quantified (see the 3% overall reduction)

actions.description: Crash thermal build. Target of 6,000 MW of new thermal in 2010 at over $5bn (Reuters, cited by Wikipedia); MercoPress, Jun 2010, reports more than 5,000 MW at $4bn in 2010. SIDOR bought 425 MW of self-generation, with the first 175 MW due by end-May 2010. No source read documents rented (as opposed to purchased) plants.
actions.lead_time_basis: No commissioning dates in sources read
actions.cost_note: $4,000M 2010 spending (MercoPress); Wikipedia/Reuters gives over $5,000M for 6,000 MW. Later National Assembly (2017) findings allege that over $80bn of about $100bn invested in the sector was embezzled.
actions.effect: Credited with rains for the June 2010 end of rationing. Existing thermal stayed degraded: Planta Centro (2,000 MW) ran only about 250-450 MW in Mar-Apr 2010.

actions.description: Reduced public-office schedules under the emergency, kept until 30 Jul 2010
actions.effect: Not quantified

outcome.blackout_or_shedding: Rolling cuts outside Caracas Jan-Jun 2010, about 3 h every 3-4 days, later about 4 h/day. Guri came within 8.79 m of collapse level on 15 Apr 2010 (Wikipedia); MercoPress says 'within 8 centimeters'.
outcome.gdp_impact: GDP contracted 3.3% in 2009 and 5.8% in Q1 2010. The power crisis was cited as prolonging the recession, but no attributable estimate was found.
outcome.what_worked: Heavy industrial curtailment (SIDOR) and the arrival of the rainy season. Reservoir rise from mid-April allowed rationing to end in June.
outcome.what_failed: Demand response was weak: 3% against a 20% target. Caracas rationing was reversed within a day. Old thermal fleet: 79% over 20 years old, 30% unavailable at end 2008. The thermal build was expensive and dogged by corruption allegations.

cases.summary: In the 'dumsor' crisis, Akosombo hovered near its minimum operating level while gas shortages and plant breakdowns compounded the hydro shortfall. Ghana ran a 24 h on / 12 h off schedule in 2015 and signed emergency and long-term thermal PPAs, including Karpowership (450 MW). The surge of take-or-pay PPAs (about 2.3 GW) later became a costly excess-capacity burden.

hydro_share_pct.note: About 55% hydro and almost 45% thermal. Akosombo alone supplies 37.5%.

cases.storage_note: Akosombo (912 MW, Volta Lake) is a very large multi-year reservoir. Its minimum operating level is 73.15 m (240 ft), and levels hovered near it in 2014-15. The record low was 71.86 m (1984).
cases.import_capacity_note: Gas imports via the West African Gas Pipeline (contracted 100m scfd, sometimes 40m; fully cut Aug 2012 to Jul 2013). Domestic gas from Atuabo came from Dec 2014.

warning.what: The WAGP gas supply was fully cut Aug 2012 to Jul 2013, and the power deficit was building in 2013 (peak demand grew 44% in 2000-09 against 7% capacity growth).
warning.basis: A structural rather than drought-only signal. No dated reservoir warning was found in the sources read.

actions.description: ECG published a load-shedding timetable from Feb 2015: residential customers got 24 h of power followed by 12 h off, and factories 6 days on and 2 days off.
actions.effect: Rationed a shortfall of available capacity (1,358 MW available in Apr 2015 against a 2,179.5 MW peak in 2014). By mid-Jul 2015 there was no fixed timetable because supply fluctuated.

actions.description: Karpowership signed a 10-year, 450 MW PPA with ECG. The first ship (Aysegul Sultan, 235 MW) arrived at Tema in 2015 (docked Dec 2015). The larger Osman Khan (470 MW) followed in 2017, burning HFO, and moved to gas at Sekondi in 2019.
actions.lead_time_basis: From PPA signing (Jun 2014) to docking in Tema (Dec 2015).
actions.cost_note: No tariff published in the sources read. In 2019 the ship burned about 2.3m barrels of HFO at USD 65.40/bbl, and the switch to domestic gas was put at about USD 120m/yr in fuel savings.
actions.effect: About a quarter of national demand (450 MW, about 26% of generation at Tema).

actions.description: The Atuabo gas processing plant (USD 900m) began commercial operation in Dec 2014. Jubilee gas reached 100m scfd by mid-Aug 2015.
actions.cost_note: Capital cost of the plant.
actions.effect: By Apr 2015, up to 80m scfd (enough for about 320 MW, against 632 MW of theoretical thermal capacity).

actions.description: PURC approved a 51.73% electricity tariff increase from 1 Jul 2015.
actions.cost_note: Government arrears to ECG were GHS 522m (about USD 144.9m) in late 2014.

actions.description: Long-term thermal PPAs totalling 2.3 GW, all with take-or-pay clauses, were signed in 2015 as a crisis response.
actions.cost_note: Later excess-capacity cost: search results (not fetched) cite the finance minister in 2019 at about USD 454m/yr for unneeded power, and a 2021 ESMAP-hosted study at USD 320-620m in capacity charges. The gas take-or-pay with GNPC (90% of Sankofa volumes) cost up to about USD 40m/month.
actions.effect: Ended the shortage (by end-2018, 19 plants with 3.9 GW dependable) but locked in overcapacity.

outcome.blackout_or_shedding: In 2015, residential customers had 12 h without power after every 24 h with it. Tema outages sometimes lasted more than 24 h.
outcome.gdp_impact: ISSER: losses of GHS 320-924m in 2014, equal to 2-6% of GDP. A later retrospective cites ISSER at close to USD 1bn and about 2 percentage points of GDP growth lost. About 13,000 jobs were lost in Jan-Apr 2015.
outcome.what_worked: Fast-deployable thermal (a powership plus domestic gas processing) restored adequacy by 2016-17. Tariff increases improved utility cash flow.
outcome.what_failed: Panic contracting of take-or-pay PPAs (2.3 GW) created a lasting excess-capacity and debt burden. The hydro shortfall was compounded by gas supply and thermal breakdowns.

cases.summary: Poor 2014/15 rains on the Zambezi and Kafue left Kariba close to its minimum operating level. ZRA cut the water allocation, and Zambia moved to 8-16 h/day load-shedding, curtailed mines and bought emergency imports at about 3.7 times the retail price. Zimbabwe (ZPC, Kariba South) also overdrew its allocation. Zimbabwe-side details were not captured (sources blocked).

hydro_share_pct.note: Kariba and Kafue Gorge supply about 90% of Zambian consumption. ZESCO produced only 1,151 MW against 2,227 MW installed (52%).

cases.storage_note: Kariba is a multi-year reservoir shared by ZESCO (North Bank, 1,080 MW) and ZPC (South Bank, 750 MW). Generation is impossible below 475.5 m. Usable storage fell to 12% in Jan 2016 from 53% a year earlier.
cases.import_capacity_note: Imports came through the SAPP from Mozambique and South Africa. In Jan 2016 Zambia asked South Africa for up to 300 MW, while Eskom was itself constrained.

warning.what: ZRA cut the ZESCO/ZPC water allocations by 12% in Mar 2015 and the generation deficit was already 560 MW. Kariba had not recharged since Jan 2015.
warning.basis: Months from the Mar 2015 ZRA cut and the 560 MW deficit to load-shedding of 8 h or more 'since summer 2015' (taken as about Jun 2015).

actions.description: ZRA cut the Kariba water allocations of ZESCO and ZPC by 12%.
actions.lead_time_basis: Reported as a March 2015 cut. No separate effective date was given.
actions.effect: Weak compliance: in Mar-Jun 2015 ZESCO overused its allocation by 39% and ZPC by 16%. ZESCO was expected to use 100% of its 2015 allocation by October. In Nov 2015 the lake was at 478.51 m, about 3 m above the 475.5 m generation floor.

actions.description: ZESCO ran nationwide rotational load-shedding.
actions.lead_time_basis: The source says 'since summer 2015'.
actions.effect: Outages of 8 to 16 hours per day. Water supply was also disrupted because pumps lost power.

actions.description: Power companies and mining firms agreed to cut mine power supply by 30%. The Copperbelt Energy Corporation supply cut was 30%, later 16%.
actions.cost_note: 1,640 workers were laid off at Mulyashi and Baluba mines (Sep 2015). A cut of 115 MW to First Quantum was said to put up to 500 jobs and USD 140m a year in government income at risk.
actions.effect: Mine load was reduced by 30% (later 16%), but no measured MW figure was found.

actions.description: ZESCO imported 148 MW of emergency power from Sep to Dec 2015. The government paid 70% of import costs and ZESCO paid up to its average selling price.
actions.cost_note: More than USD 40m for 148 MW from Sep to Dec 2015. Imports cost 18.34 USc/kWh, against a 5 USc/kWh domestic selling price. In ZESCO's accounts, net import costs were K511m in 2015 against K36m in 2014, and the government disbursed K352m (70% of import costs). The kwacha figures were not converted.
actions.effect: Partial offset of a deficit that reached 985 MW (Sep 2015) to 1,000 MW. ZESCO's interest cover fell to 1.4x (13x in 2014).

actions.description: Zambia asked South Africa for up to 300 MW of emergency power.
actions.effect: No outcome found.

actions.description: A planned Turkish powership of 200 MW to be moored off Nacala, Mozambique, supplying Zambia via the regional grid. A ZESCO statement shown in a search snippet (not fetched) gave 100 MW from Karpowership, Mozambique, from 15 Mar 2016.
actions.lead_time_basis: Reported as planned in Feb 2016. No delivery date was confirmed in the sources read.

actions.description: A new mining tariff of 10.35 USc/kWh was proposed, more than double the estimated cost of production. Tariffs were described as 'rapidly ratcheting up'.
actions.cost_note: Proposed tariff level, not a cost.

outcome.blackout_or_shedding: 8-16 h/day load-shedding in Zambia from mid-2015. The deficit grew from 560 MW (Mar 2015) to 985 MW (Sep 2015) and about 1,000 MW (Feb 2016). Kariba usable storage was 12% in Jan 2016.
outcome.duration_basis: Mid-2015 to at least Feb/Mar 2016, from sources dated Jan-Feb 2016. The end date was not established.
outcome.gdp_impact: Zambian growth fell to 3.4% from about 7% (with copper prices down 18% at the same time). 2016 growth was projected at a little over half the 7% target and the deficit at 8.1% of GDP.
outcome.what_worked: Government co-funding of costly imports limited shedding. Curtailing mine load spread the shortfall.
outcome.what_failed: The 12% allocation cut was not enforced: both utilities overdrew their allocations, and the lake fell to within about 3 m of the generation floor. Imports at 18 USc/kWh against 5 USc/kWh retail were financially unsustainable. Delayed new capacity (Itezhi-Tezhi 120 MW, Maamba 300 MW, both slipped from 2014) left no buffer.

cases.summary: The 2015-16 El Nino, a 1-in-50-year drought with rainfall 40% below normal, combined with a February 2016 fire that took out the 560 MW Guatape hydro plant and with thermal-plant problems. Colombia came close to programmed blackouts. It avoided rationing with heavy thermal dispatch (55% of generation by April), LNG and Ecuador imports, a spot-price cap and the 6-week 'Apagar Paga' bonus/penalty savings campaign.

hydro_share_pct.note: Energy mix 77% hydro and 18% thermal (WEC/ANDEG). Hydro was 71% of installed capacity (Inter-American Dialogue).

cases.storage_note: Seasonal reservoirs. Water reserve was about 41% at El Nino onset and fell to 26% after the Guatape incident (WEC).
cases.import_capacity_note: Interconnection with Ecuador. Imports peaked at 5.6 GWh (March 2016) and were about 2% of supply.

warning.what: Spot prices jumped in Sep-Oct 2015 above the scarcity price, and the regulator adjusted the scarcity price in Sep 2015. The El Nino drought deepened over the Sep-Dec 2015 wet season.
warning.basis: From the Sep 2015 price spike and scarcity-price change (WEC, Figure 1) to the Guatape fire and acute shortage in Feb 2016.

actions.description: Maximum dispatch of thermal plants backed by Firm Energy Obligations under the reliability charge.
actions.lead_time_basis: Existing plants dispatched as prices rose.
actions.cost_note: The scarcity price was capped at about US$100/MWh (the source prints 'US$100/kWh'), while generation cost was almost 7x higher. Thermal companies lost about US$250m. Spot prices exceeded US$400/MWh, against US$30-50 normally. (No per-MWh generation cost given; the US$400/MWh is the spot-price peak.)
actions.effect: Thermal reached 55% of generation by April 2016, about 100 GWh/day. Some plants failed: a Zona Franca Celsia unit was damaged and there were operational problems.

actions.description: Spot-price cap at 75% of the first level of the incremental operating cost of rationing. A temporary 6-month floor on the scarcity price to help generators cover costs, with extra floors for oil and diesel plants.
actions.lead_time_basis: Exact dates not stated in the WEC case study.
actions.cost_note: Costs passed largely to end users. Distribution companies without hedges were hurt.
actions.effect: Kept thermal generators running despite losses.

actions.description: 'Apagar Paga' (turning off pays), backed by CREG Resolution 029/2016 (published 7 Mar 2016) for March-April 2016. It credited users who consumed below their baseline (reportedly Feb 2016 consumption) and charged those above it, about 'one peso of incentive per peso saved, one peso charged per peso not saved' (EPM). Daily target: save at least 5%, 400 GWh over 6 weeks. Supported by intense communication. Ended by CREG Resolution 051/2016 (23 Apr 2016).
actions.lead_time_basis: Resolution published 7 Mar 2016; campaign live within days.
actions.cost_note: Net bill credits and charges not found. La Republica valued users' savings at about COP 417,910 million, using a spot price of COP 850/kWh minus about COP 60 reliability charge.
actions.effect: 1,179 GWh saved by 17 Apr 2016 against the 400 GWh goal (President Santos). Daily savings reached 5.88% when it ended. Reservoir drawdown was 22 GWh/day against the 48 GWh/day XM model projection. Single-day peak saving was 24.51% on Good Friday. The WEC/UN case study says it cut demand 5%.

actions.description: More gas supply via LNG imported from the Caribbean.
actions.lead_time_basis: No dates found.
actions.cost_note: Not found.
actions.effect: Not quantified.

actions.description: Additional energy imports from Ecuador via the existing interconnection.
actions.lead_time_basis: Existing link, used after the Guatape shutdown.
actions.cost_note: Not found.
actions.effect: Peak 5.6 GWh (in a day) in March 2016, about 2% of supply.

actions.description: Public buildings switched off power at 6 pm. Industry self-generation contributed more than 140 MW.
actions.lead_time_basis: No dates found.
actions.cost_note: Not found.
actions.effect: More than 140 MW of self-generation.

actions.description: Fast-tracked licensing of thermal expansion. Long-term: two new thermal plants (100 MW gas, 260 MW coal) by 2018 and renewables diversification (2019).
actions.lead_time_basis: From 2016 to plant entry in 2018.
actions.cost_note: Not found.
actions.effect: Structural, not for this crisis.

outcome.blackout_or_shedding: No rationing or programmed blackouts. A shortage of about 200 MW was reached in April 2016. XM and the National Operations Council had recommended programmed 5% cuts, which were averted by voluntary savings.
outcome.gdp_impact: Not found. Costs fell on end users through spot prices and on thermal generators, which lost about US$250m.
outcome.what_worked: The reliability-charge capacity market secured thermal backup. Apagar Paga's symmetric bonus/penalty plus strong communication produced savings far above target within weeks. Ecuador imports, LNG and coordination with the IDEAM met agency also helped. Fedesarrollo credits the post-1994 reforms with avoiding rationing.
outcome.what_failed: The campaign launched late (March 2016). The scarcity-price formula was tied to oil prices, so after the oil crash generators produced at a loss. Government was slow to resolve the price issue, thermal plants failed operationally, and there was no contingency for the Guatape fire, which took about 4% of national capacity offline. Guatape was not expected back at full output until Sep 2017.

cases.summary: After three years of rainfall 50-65% below normal, Guri fell to a historic low of about 242 m, near its 240 m minimum. The government gave public workers Fridays off, then a two-day work week, imposed 4 h/day rotating cuts for 40 days, closed schools on Fridays, and moved clocks forward 30 minutes. Measures eased in mid-June as rain raised Guri.

hydro_share_pct.note: Guri alone: more than 60% (Circle of Blue) and 60% (AP/Fox); AFP says 70%. Total hydro share not given.

cases.storage_note: Guri (10,323 MW) is a very large reservoir. It was at about 242 m on 22 Apr 2016, near the 240 m minimum operating level. In late April it was falling 10 cm/day, down from 20 cm/day.
cases.import_capacity_note: No emergency imports reported in sources read

warning.what: A multi-year deficit: rainfall 50-65% below normal for three years (Ministry of Electricity). Guri reached a historic low of 242 m by 22 Apr 2016.
warning.basis: No dated first warning found in sources read

actions.description: Most of about 2.8M state employees had Fridays off in April-May 2016. From 28 Apr, Wednesday-Friday were non-working days for the public sector (two-day week, full pay), extended on 30 May for two weeks, and ended 14 Jun 2016. Schools were closed on Fridays.
actions.lead_time_basis: Two-day week effective the day after the 27 Apr announcement
actions.effect: Not quantified in sources read

actions.description: Rotating 4 h/day cuts for 40 days (or until Guri recovered) from 25 Apr 2016 in most of the country. Caracas and four other states were spared, the oil sector was expected to be exempt, and there were no cuts 20:00-24:00. Weekend cuts were suspended in mid-June and rationing was later lifted.
actions.lead_time_basis: From the 21-22 Apr announcement to the 25 Apr start
actions.effect: Guri's daily decline slowed from 20 cm to 10 cm by 27 Apr, which Maduro attributed to the measures

actions.description: Permanent time-zone change: clocks moved forward 30 minutes to UTC-4 at 02:30 on 1 May 2016, reversing the half-hour change set by Chavez, to add evening daylight at peak demand
actions.lead_time_basis: Announced mid/late April 2016, effective 1 May 2016
actions.effect: No savings estimate given

actions.description: Power to manufacturers curtailed. Shopping malls ordered to supply their own generation.
actions.effect: Not quantified

actions.description: Public appeals to cut appliance use (e.g. hairdryers)
actions.lead_time_basis: Immediate
actions.effect: Not quantified

outcome.blackout_or_shedding: 4 h/day rotating cuts from 25 Apr 2016 outside Caracas and four states; weekend cuts suspended mid-June; rationing later lifted
outcome.gdp_impact: Not quantified in sources read. It came during a broader economic collapse with shortages and looting.
outcome.what_worked: Drastic demand suppression (public sector closed three days a week, rotating cuts) slowed Guri's drawdown and avoided falling below 240 m until rains came
outcome.what_failed: There were no supply-side emergency options in the sources read. Rain in May was not enough to refill the reservoir, and the shortened work week had to be extended on 30 May.

cases.summary: Drought in the first months of 2019 cut hydro generation roughly in half; with all thermal plants including high-cost gas turbines already at maximum, the CEB imposed scheduled daily power cuts of up to 4 hours from late March until 11 April 2019. The government then declared an emergency under the Electricity Act and contracted 400 MW of barge-mounted power without competitive tender.

hydro_share_pct.note: major hydro excluding mini hydro, 2018; fell to 23.8% in 2019 (CBSL). Press reported hydro down to ~15% of production during the crisis.

cases.storage_note: Mahaweli and Laxapana cascade reservoirs, shared with irrigation and drinking water; seasonal storage dependent on monsoons. Cuts were partly aimed at keeping reservoirs above minimum operating levels.
cases.import_capacity_note: Island grid with no international interconnection.

warning.what: Dry weather prevailed through the first seven months of 2019; hydro dropped drastically towards end-Q1 2019
warning.basis: No dated early warning found in sources read; recurrent drought shortfalls had prompted emergency purchases in 2016-2017 as well

actions.description: CEB ran all thermal plants, including high-cost gas turbines, at maximum capacity.
actions.lead_time_basis: immediate dispatch
actions.cost_note: 2019 average CEB cost: fuel oil LKR 31.93/kWh vs hydro LKR 2.49/kWh; fuel-oil generation +38.2% to 5,016 GWh; CEB pre-tax loss LKR 85.4bn in 2019 vs LKR 30.5bn in 2018
actions.effect: Insufficient on its own; load shedding still required

actions.description: Scheduled daily power cuts (up to 4 hours/day) from 22-25 March 2019 through early April; the ministry said it had not approved the cuts and PUCSL threatened legal action over unscheduled cuts.
actions.lead_time_basis: immediate
actions.effect: Kept supply balanced and reservoirs above minimum levels until rains; cuts ended 11 April 2019

actions.description: Attempt to induce artificial rain over catchments.
actions.effect: No effect on reservoir levels reported

actions.description: Cabinet declared an emergency under the Sri Lanka Electricity Act (allowing purchase without competitive tender) and approved 400 MW from two 200 MW barge-mounted plants from a Turkish supplier: Kerawalapitiya for 6 months from June 2019, Galle for 9 months from September 2019; price capped by Finance Ministry.
actions.lead_time_basis: crisis start March 2019 to first barge supply June 2019; Galle unit 6 months after crisis, dependent on ~3 months of transmission works
actions.cost_note: LKR 26.20 per unit (kWh), i.e. LKR 26,200/MWh; not converted (no sourced exchange rate). Arrived only after the cuts had ended.
actions.effect: No measured effect on the March-April shortage, which ended with rains before delivery

outcome.blackout_or_shedding: Scheduled daily cuts of up to 4 h, ~22 March to 11 April 2019
outcome.gdp_impact: No official estimate found; CBSL notes industry and services activity were affected; CEB pre-tax loss rose to LKR 85.4bn (from 30.5bn) on thermal reliance
outcome.what_worked: Rotational cuts kept reservoirs above minimum levels until rain returned; maximum thermal dispatch.
outcome.what_failed: Repeated failure to add firm capacity (emergency purchases also in 2016-17) left no reserve margin; emergency barges were contracted after the crisis, without tender and with grid-absorption concerns; heavy financial losses to CEB.

cases.source_notes: 2019 chosen over 2016 (2016 cuts were driven by Norochcholai coal breakdowns; drought response then was a 55-65 MW emergency purchase). Reuters 2019 story (Dhaka Tribune/PreventionWeb mirrors) returned 403; ministry/PUCSL dispute and 25 March start are from search extracts. One press report cites LKR 24.80/unit for the barges; Daily FT (fetched) says LKR 26.20. 2022 crisis was fuel/FX driven and excluded.

cases.summary: In the first half of 2021, a La Nina dry spell in the South Island coincided with falling gas output from the Pohokura field. Hydro storage fell about 2,000 GWh below 2020 levels and the system leaned on coal at Huntly. Rain in May ended the energy risk. The 9 Aug 2021 cuts to about 34,000 customers were a winter-peak capacity and coordination failure that reviews said 'need not have happened', not a hydro energy shortage. The dry-year problem later led to the Lake Onslow pumped-hydro study (cancelled) and a 10-year Huntly coal strategic reserve.

hydro_share_pct.note: Hydro share not extracted; renewables were 82.1% of 43,267 GWh generated in 2021

cases.storage_note: Hydro lakes, mostly in the South Island, hold only weeks-to-months of storage, which makes the 'dry year problem' structural. Thermal backup is Huntly (coal/gas, Rankine units of 250 MW each) and gas plants.
cases.import_capacity_note: Isolated grid with no international interconnection; the HVDC link joins the North and South Islands only. The fuel backstop is imported coal: 1.85 Mt (38.6 PJ) in 2021, +69%, a record.

warning.what: Genesis: hydro storage 'significantly below average', about 2,000 GWh below the same time in 2020 (2020 being the driest winter on record)
warning.basis: From the 15 Feb 2021 Genesis release to Mar/Apr 2021, when generators started diverting gas from industry (EA dry-year review page); the risk ended with rain in May 2021

actions.description: Genesis made its third 250 MW Huntly Rankine unit (Unit 2) available from 22 Feb to 30 Sep 2021, to run alongside Rankine Units 1 and 4 and gas Units 5 and 6
actions.lead_time_basis: Announced 15 Feb, available 22 Feb 2021
actions.cost_note: Not disclosed; the average 2021 wholesale price was nearly double 2020's
actions.effect: Coal use for electricity generation rose 29.5% in 2021

actions.description: Record coal imports for Huntly, plus deals to divert natural gas from industrial users to power generation (Mar/Apr 2021)
actions.cost_note: Not disclosed
actions.effect: Coal imports +69% to 1.85 Mt; NZ became a net coal importer for the first time since 1990

actions.description: After the 9 Aug 2021 event: Electricity Authority Phase 1 (Sep 2021) and Phase 2 (Apr 2022) reviews; a ministerial (MBIE) investigation with 18 recommendations; a Rulings Panel complaint against the system operator; industry grid-emergency simulation (26 May 2022); better system operator communications; EA dry-year review changed security-of-supply forecasting and emergency management policy
actions.lead_time_basis: Event 9 Aug 2021 to industry simulation 26 May 2022
actions.effect: Process and governance changes; not quantified

actions.description: NZ Battery Project: studied Lake Onslow pumped hydro as long-duration dry-year storage. Phase 1 cost estimate rose to NZD 15.7 bn (from about NZD 4 bn); delivery no earlier than the mid-2030s. The new government scrapped it in Dec 2023.
actions.lead_time_basis: Construction up to 9 years after a final decision; never built
actions.cost_note: NZD 15.7 bn estimate (Mar 2023), not converted
actions.effect: None; cancelled

actions.description: Strategic Energy Reserve / Huntly Firming Option: Genesis, Contact, Meridian and Mercury fund a 600,000-tonne coal stockpile and pay Genesis a fee to keep Rankine Unit 2 as dry-year cover for 10 years. The Commerce Commission authorised it in Nov 2025. The unit had been due to retire.
actions.lead_time_basis: Announced Aug 2025, authorised 6 Nov 2025
actions.cost_note: Fee not disclosed
actions.effect: Prompted by a dry year in 2024 that pushed wholesale prices sharply higher

outcome.blackout_or_shedding: 9 Aug 2021: about 34,000 customers cut without warning for up to 2 hours on one of the coldest nights; Waikato hardest hit. The reviews found there was enough discretionary load to avoid it. The dry-year energy shortage itself caused no rationing (rain arrived in May 2021).
outcome.what_worked: Thermal and coal backstop at Huntly (third Rankine unit, record coal imports) carried the system through the dry months; operators avoided automatic under-frequency load shedding on 9 Aug.
outcome.what_failed: Coordination and communication by the system operator, which had poor visibility of discretionary load; heavy reliance on imported coal; the long-term storage option (Lake Onslow) proved too costly and was cancelled.

cases.summary: After the driest wet season in 91 years (Nov 2020-Apr 2021), Brazil avoided rationing. It dispatched all thermal plants, imported expensive power from Argentina and Uruguay, relaxed reservoir and transmission constraints, set up a ministerial crisis chamber (CREG), added a 'water scarcity' tariff flag and paid voluntary demand-reduction bonuses. Consumers carried the cost through tariffs and a later loan.

hydro_share_pct.note: No 2021 hydro share found in the sources read.

cases.storage_note: Large multi-year reservoirs. The Southeast/Midwest subsystem holds about 70% of reservoir storage, and its reservoirs fell to about 27% by July 2021 (S&P, search excerpt).
cases.enso_note: Sources read do not attribute the 2020-21 drought to an ENSO phase.
cases.import_capacity_note: Interconnections with Argentina and Uruguay, plus Itaipu (Paraguay). Imports were 1.01% of national consumption in 2021, up from 0.52% in 2020 (CCEE via Rio Times).

warning.what: Thermal dispatch rose from Oct 2020 and marginal operating costs hit their highest level since 2015. On about 27 May 2021 the Electric Sector Monitoring Committee (CMSE) issued a 'water risk' warning and the met service issued a water-emergency alert for the Parana basin.
warning.basis: From the Oct 2020 rise in thermal dispatch (S&P, search excerpt) to the peak-risk months Sep-Oct 2021. The formal alert in May 2021 was about 4 months before the peak.

actions.description: Dispatch of the whole thermal fleet, including the most expensive plants (variable costs up to about R$2,400-2,500/MWh), from late 2020 through 2021. Government authorised exceptional thermal use.
actions.lead_time_basis: Existing plants, dispatched immediately.
actions.cost_note: R$16.8bn through Oct 2021 (MME) for thermal generation plus imports, related charges and hydro-displacement compensation. Converted at an assumed 5.4 BRL/USD (approximate 2021 average, not from a cited source). In July MME had projected R$13.1bn through Nov. Idec projected R$28.4bn of extra generation cost passed through tariff flags in 2021. Variable cost up to R$2,400-2,500/MWh at the most expensive plants.
actions.effect: Avoided rationing and kept supply secure in 2021. The Conta Bandeiras deficit reached R$12.01bn by Oct 2021.
actions.cost_estimate_basis: USD figures converted by the researcher at an assumed 5.4 BRL/USD that is not from a cited source: treat USD values as estimates; BRL values in cost_note are as reported.

actions.description: Energy purchases from Argentina and Uruguay at high prices.
actions.lead_time_basis: No dates found for the decision.
actions.cost_note: Jan-Oct 2021: Argentina US$670m (+7,504% compared with the same period of 2020), Uruguay US$266m. Prices: Uruguay up to R$1,796 (US$320)/MWh, Argentina R$1,534/MWh, against R$196/MWh for Itaipu.
actions.effect: Imports rose to 1.01% of national consumption (from 0.52% in 2020).
actions.cost_estimate_basis: USD figures converted by the researcher at an assumed 5.4 BRL/USD that is not from a cited source: treat USD values as estimates; BRL values in cost_note are as reported.

actions.description: Crisis chamber CREG (Camara de Regras Excepcionais para Gestao Hidroenergetica) created by MP 1.055 of 28 Jun 2021. It was chaired by the Minister of Mines and Energy and could order changes to reservoir and hydro-plant flows. First meeting 1 Jul 2021. It was extinguished when the MP lapsed unvoted on 7 Nov 2021.
actions.lead_time_basis: MP 28 Jun 2021, first meeting 1 Jul 2021.
actions.cost_note: n/a
actions.effect: Centralised emergency decisions, including the escassez hidrica flag (CREG Res. 3, 31 Aug 2021).

actions.description: ONS and partner bodies (35 lines of action) relaxed hydraulic restrictions and transmission limits. This included more flexible minimum outflows at Jupia, Porto Primavera, Ilha Solteira and Tres Irmaos, and reduced outflows in the Sao Francisco cascade.
actions.lead_time_basis: No dates found.
actions.cost_note: Saving rather than cost: R$26.9bn in operating cost over the 2020-21 crisis, of which about R$15.8bn was consumer benefit from avoiding thermal plants with variable cost up to R$2,500/MWh (ONS).
actions.effect: Preserved about 4.1% of Southeast/Midwest stored energy.

actions.description: Tariff flags escalated: red flag 1 (R$4.16/100 kWh) in May 2021 and red flag 2 (R$6.24/100 kWh) in June. Red flag 2 was later R$9.49/100 kWh. A new 'escassez hidrica' flag of R$14.20/100 kWh, set by CREG Resolution 3 of 31 Aug 2021, applied 1 Sep 2021 to 30 Apr 2022 to fund thermal dispatch and imports.
actions.lead_time_basis: Decided 31 Aug 2021, effective 1 Sep 2021.
actions.cost_note: R$142/MWh surcharge on regulated consumers (R$14.20 per 100 kWh). MegaWatt consultancy estimated R$18/100 kWh would have been needed to avoid a deficit. ANEEL loan to distributors of up to R$10.8bn (Conta Escassez Hidrica, decree of 14 Jan 2022) to avoid a 21% tariff rise in 2022.
actions.effect: Cost recovery more than demand signal. Even so, the flag account ran a deficit.

actions.description: Voluntary Demand Response (RVD) for large and free consumers and aggregators, run by ONS. Offers were hourly blocks of 4-7 hours, at least 5 MW, valid 1-6 months, and paid via the short-term market, with the cost above the spot price (PLD) recovered through the system-service charge (ESS). Participants had to deliver at least 80% to be paid. Announced Aug 2021 (Portaria 22, 23 Aug 2021).
actions.lead_time_basis: Rules published 23-31 Aug 2021, operating in September.
actions.cost_note: No programme cost found.
actions.effect: Industry committed an average 237 MW reduction at peak hours in September 2021 (ONS). ONS suspended new offers in early Nov 2021 as rains returned.

actions.description: Consumer bonus for voluntary reduction: R$50 per 100 kWh saved for an average reduction of 10-20% against 2020 consumption, Sep-Dec 2021 bills. The bonus was credited on January 2022 bills.
actions.lead_time_basis: Rules late Aug 2021, counting from Sep 2021 bills.
actions.cost_note: R$2.4bn in bonuses (MME), converted at an assumed 5.4 BRL/USD (not from a cited source). Unit cost: R$500/MWh (R$50 per 100 kWh) is about US$93/MWh at the same rate, compared with R$1,500-2,500/MWh for imports or the most expensive thermal.
actions.effect: 5.6 TWh saved Sep-Dec 2021, 2.7% of consumption in the same period of 2020. MME says this lowered residential tariffs by about 4.5%. In an Ipec survey, 71% had not heard of the programme.
actions.cost_estimate_basis: USD figures converted by the researcher at an assumed 5.4 BRL/USD that is not from a cited source: treat USD values as estimates; BRL values in cost_note are as reported.

outcome.blackout_or_shedding: No rationing or load shedding.
outcome.gdp_impact: Not found. The cost fell on electricity tariffs: R$16.8bn in measures through Oct 2021, flag deficits and a loan of up to R$10.8bn.
outcome.what_worked: Thermal and import capacity existed and could be dispatched. Relaxing hydraulic constraints saved about R$27bn in operating cost. Voluntary demand bonuses cost much less per MWh than marginal thermal.
outcome.what_failed: Late, expensive response and weak communication (71% unaware of the bonus). The flag was too low to cover costs, so deficits were rolled into a loan repaid by future tariffs. An Instituto E+ study argues that crisis costs since 2001 could have been about 60% lower with robust demand response and a 4-5% consumption cut instead of reliance on thermal plants.

cases.summary: Severe drought cut California hydro output in 2021 to 48% below the 10-year average. Lake Oroville's Hyatt plant went offline on 5 Aug 2021 for about five months. Gas generation and imports filled the gap. The state then built a $3.4 bn Strategic Reliability Reserve, which helped carry the record Sep 2022 heat-wave peak with no rotating outages.

hydro_share_pct.note: EIA model: summer (Jun-Sep) hydro share 15% with median water vs 8% in the 2022 drought case

cases.storage_note: Large multi-purpose reservoirs (Shasta, Oroville) are run mainly for water supply and environmental and agricultural needs, with power secondary. Hydro is a minority of supply; imports are about one-third of supply.
cases.import_capacity_note: Imports are nearly one-third of California's power supply (EIA); the state is part of the Western interconnection.

warning.what: Record-low monthly hydro generation in May-June 2021 amid statewide drought (41% of the state in exceptional drought by Aug 2021)
warning.basis: Drought already severe in spring 2021; Hyatt went offline 5 Aug 2021. The 'record low May/June' detail comes from a search summary of S&P/EIA, not a page read; the drought share is from EIA.

actions.description: More in-state gas generation and imports from neighbouring markets to replace lost hydro (2021-22)
actions.lead_time_basis: Market dispatch responds immediately
actions.cost_note: EIA 2022 drought case: Western wholesale prices +5% and California energy CO2 +6% vs the median-water case; gas rises from 45% to 50% of the summer mix
actions.effect: Lost hydro covered without energy shortage

actions.description: Electric Supply Strategic Reliability Reserve Program (DWR, $2.4 bn, part of the AB 205 reserve of $3.4 bn over 5 years): temporary diesel generators, new storage, reimbursing utilities for imports, and life extension of three once-through-cooling gas plants
actions.lead_time_basis: AB 205 (Chapter 61 of 2022) passed mid-2022; the program delivered MW in the Sep 2022 heat event. The June decision month is an estimate.
actions.cost_note: OTC plants: 2,859 MW for 2024-2026 at up to $1.9 bn, roughly $220/kW-yr (estimate: 1,900 / (2,859 MW x 3 yr))
actions.effect: Provided 554-1,416 MW during the Sep 2022 extreme heat event

actions.description: Demand Side Grid Support (CEC, $295M) pays customers to cut use at summer evening peaks and in emergencies (enrolment started summer 2022); utility demand response including the Emergency Load Reduction Program was activated on 6 Sep 2022. Distributed Electricity Backup Assets ($695M) was still being developed.
actions.lead_time_basis: Funded by AB 205 mid-2022 with enrolment in summer 2022
actions.cost_note: DSGS allocation over 5 years; DEBA a further $695M
actions.effect: Not separately quantified in the sources read

actions.description: CAISO Flex Alerts (voluntary conservation 4-9 pm) plus a statewide Wireless Emergency Alert text from CalOES on 6 Sep 2022, issued alongside an EEA3 declaration
actions.lead_time_basis: Same-day
actions.cost_note: Essentially free
actions.effect: Within 5 minutes of the text alert, demand fell by more than 2,100 MW below the hour-ahead forecast and stayed below it until 9 pm; record peak 51,426 MW

outcome.blackout_or_shedding: No rotating outages in 2021-22 according to the sources read. EEA3 declared 6 Sep 2022. Hyatt was offline 5 Aug 2021 to about Jan 2022 (about five months) and restarted at about 30 MW.
outcome.what_worked: Deep import and gas backstop; quickly funded strategic reserve; emergency text alert gave a fast, large demand drop.
outcome.what_failed: Drought exposed reliance on hydro and imports during heat events; higher emissions and prices; the reserve relies on diesel and on extending old gas plants.

cases.summary: After more than a decade of megadrought, reservoir energy in 2021 stood near half the long-run average and hydro fell to about 13% of generation; in August 2021 the government issued a preventive rationing decree (DS 51) that ring-fenced reservoir water, later as a 650 GWh hydro reserve, while coal, diesel and LNG filled the gap. Rationing quotas were never needed in the sources read, and the reserve was progressively released from mid-2022 as hydrology improved.

hydro_share_pct.note: April 2021 monthly share (run-of-river plus reservoir), lowest in decades; on 12 Aug 2021 hydro was 12.6% vs thermal 73.5% of daily generation

cases.storage_note: Seasonal reservoirs (Ralco, Laguna del Maule, Lago Laja, Colbun, Rapel) shared with irrigation agreements plus run-of-river; reservoir stored energy ~48% of the 1994-2020 average in mid-2021; hydrological exceedance 96.8% (driest ~3%).
cases.enso_note: 2021-22 La Nina years; sources read attribute shortfall to persistent megadrought and low snowmelt, not explicitly ENSO.
cases.import_capacity_note: No significant electricity interconnection; pipeline gas from Argentina sought from October 2021 to complement LNG imports.

warning.what: April 2021 hydro share 13% (lowest in decades), reservoir energy ~48% of average, hydrological exceedance 96.8%
warning.basis: June 2021 publication of April data to the 16-18 Aug 2021 decree

actions.description: Preventive rationing decree DS 51/2021 (signed 16 Aug, published 18 Aug 2021 under LGSE art. 163, after the CNE technical report of 13 Aug): system operator (Coordinador) must avoid using water stored as of 13 Aug 2021, use conservative inflow forecasts, and restrict reservoir hydro in ancillary-service auctions. DS 29/2022 (22 Mar 2022) set a hydro reserve of 650 GWh to be held at all times; DS 66/2022 began releasing it; CNE in Aug 2022 recommended cutting it to 66 GWh. Decree extended to 30 Sep 2022 and later to 30 Sep 2023.
actions.lead_time_basis: decree effective on publication
actions.cost_note: Implicit cost is extra thermal/diesel dispatch; not quantified
actions.effect: Built reserve in Ralco, Laguna del Maule, Lago Laja; by Aug 2022 Coordinador returned 48 GWh (Maule) and 102 GWh (Ralco) due to spill risk; worst-case projected deficit Aug 2022-Jun 2023 was 294.8 GWh

actions.description: Coordinador brought retired coal unit Ventanas 1 (120 MW) back from reserve; Bocamina 2 (350 MW), earmarked for closure, could be kept in service; diesel dispatch rose sharply.
actions.lead_time_basis: reported in operation by 13 Aug 2021
actions.cost_note: No $/MWh found
actions.effect: Thermal 73.5% of generation on 12 Aug 2021; power-sector diesel use ~4,000 m3/day (12% of thermal generation) vs 1.7% of thermal Jan-Jul 2020

actions.description: Decree required LNG generators to maximise regasification and LNG transport capacity; generators to report fuel-related unavailability; diesel requirement projections in m3/day (DS 1/2022); Chile sought additional Argentine pipeline gas from October 2021.
actions.lead_time_basis: Argentine gas targeted from October 2021
actions.effect: Not quantified

actions.description: Voltage reduction: distributors to operate at the lowest voltage within quality standards, after submitting estimated savings to the regulator (SEC); also optimisation/postponement of major maintenance, reduced transmission security margins on some segments, and a register of customers' backup generation.
actions.lead_time_basis: subject to distributor implementation plans; timing not found
actions.effect: Not quantified

actions.description: Public saving campaigns announced alongside the decree; decree framework to stimulate or reward voluntary savings.
actions.effect: Not quantified

outcome.blackout_or_shedding: No supply cuts reported in sources read; rationing quota mechanism in DS 51 was available but no evidence of activation found; CNE (Aug 2022) projected no unserved energy north of Ciruelos for 2022
outcome.what_worked: Pre-emptive legal framework (art. 163 decree) letting the operator ring-fence reservoir energy months ahead; large thermal fleet plus fast-growing solar/wind (~10 GW) as backup; reserve sized and later released as hydrology improved.
outcome.what_failed: Reliance on coal and diesel ran counter to decarbonisation (retired coal unit restarted); reserve accumulation conflicted with irrigation agreements and spill risk at Ralco/Maule; diesel logistics (~3,500 m3/day non-pipeline limit) became a binding constraint.

cases.source_notes: Extension to 30 Sep 2023 from search extracts of CNE/Diario Oficial listings, not full text. No annual 2021 hydro share, cost of extra thermal, or $/MWh found; hydro generation reported down 30.1% in 2021 vs 2020 in a search extract (infraestructurapublica.cl), not fetched.

cases.summary: A dry year left reservoirs in southern Norway (NO1, NO2, NO5) far below median just as the European gas crisis pushed up prices on the interconnectors. NO2 prices hit records and rationing was openly discussed. The response was asking producers to hold back water, an export-limit mechanism linked to reservoir levels, and a large household bill subsidy. No rationing happened.

hydro_share_pct.note: 'around 90%' of electricity output (Reuters via Zawya); not a precise 2022 statistic

cases.storage_note: Total Norwegian reservoir capacity 87,204 GWh, of which NO2 (south-west) 33,899 GWh and NO1 5,976 GWh (NVE). Seasonal and multi-season storage; inflow is very low in winter.
